steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on ARTiST, a system that uses an LLM to automatically simplify text instructions for task guidance on AR head-mounted displays. It should motivate the problem, explain the approach and the user studies, and end with a list of contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- AR and its use for task guidance
- HMDs and the problem of long text in a small field of view
- Text simplification and why existing methods don't fit AR
- Our approach: formative study and the ARTiST system
- Evaluation studies and results
- Contributions

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Augmented reality (AR) has become a transformative technology that is used in many domains, such as education, entertainment, collaborative work, and professional training. AR puts digital content on top of the physical world in real-time, and this helps people do tasks more efficiently. Because of this, AR applications are used more and more for task guidance, for example in manufacturing, education, and surgery. In the manufacturing industry AR devices are widely adopted, for example so that workers rely less on guidance materials or other devices that are outside of the immediate work environment.

A head-mounted display (HMD) is one type of AR device. It allows multi-modal interactions while the user keeps focus on the immediate work environment. Since they are hands-free, HMDs are often used for text-based task guidance. But HMDs have a relatively small field of view (FoV) compared to desktop displays, and this limits how much text they can show. Longer instructions can occlude the user's view, and this results in lower productivity and higher cognitive load, and also safety risks. So text-based instructions in AR need to be optimized to be more useful.

One potential solution is text simplification. Text simplification has been used to reduce the complexity or length of text for users in non-AR settings, so that it is easier to understand. However, as far as we know there are no established methods for adapting and simplifying text for the specific context of AR. There are also several concerns with applying the existing methods to AR. First, traditional text simplification methods usually aim to help comprehension for people with limited reading skills, and this audience may not overlap with AR users. Second, these methods were not designed or fine-tuned for AR-specific constraints, like the small FoV, the restricted display area, or the fact that users need to do physical tasks while they read. Third, text simplification is an opportunity to use spatial information in AR content, by describing a physical object's color, location, or direction. For example, saying the location of a physical object in the text can help users execute tasks in AR.

- Our approach
  - goal: tailor existing methods to AR; reduce cognitive load, improve task performance
  - prior work + own formative study (literature survey, open-ended exploration, expert interview)
  - findings: long-text reading challenges (cognitive load), comprehension
  - three design guidelines -> ARTiST
  - few-shot prompting; multi-task capabilities of LLM GPT-3; no extensively annotated data
  - prompts based on chain-of-thought
  - two novel methods: "plan-of-technique" prompt, "error-aware" model calibration
- Evaluation
  - two studies, 16 participants
  - study 1: pour-over coffee, meeting room setup by criteria
  - study 2: video editing on iPad, AR instructions via HMD
  - compare to unmodified text and existing methods: performance metrics, cognitive load, subjective ratings
  - results: fewer errors, more steps correctly memorized, lower cognitive load
- Contributions
  - ARTiST (few-shot prompts, customized GPT-3, chain-of-thought, plan-of-technique, error-aware calibration)
  - formative study: lit review, open-ended exploration with seven participants, interview with three field experts; design guidelines
  - 16-participant evaluation vs baseline and existing methods: fewer errors, lower cognitive load, higher ratings (readability, memorability, guidance, trust)
  - open-source implementation

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Augmented reality (AR) has become a transformative technology that is used in many domains, such as education, entertainment, collaborative work, and professional training. AR puts digital content on top of the physical world in real-time, and this helps people do tasks more efficiently. Because of this, AR applications are used more and more for task guidance, for example in manufacturing, education, and surgery. In the manufacturing industry AR devices are widely adopted, for example so that workers rely less on guidance materials or other devices that are outside of the immediate work environment.

A head-mounted display (HMD) is one type of AR device. It allows multi-modal interactions while the user keeps focus on the immediate work environment. Since they are hands-free, HMDs are often used for text-based task guidance. But HMDs have a relatively small field of view (FoV) compared to desktop displays, and this limits how much text they can show. Longer instructions can occlude the user's view, and this results in lower productivity and higher cognitive load, and also safety risks. So text-based instructions in AR need to be optimized to be more useful.

One potential solution is text simplification. Text simplification has been used to reduce the complexity or length of text for users in non-AR settings, so that it is easier to understand. However, as far as we know there are no established methods for adapting and simplifying text for the specific context of AR. There are also several concerns with applying the existing methods to AR. First, traditional text simplification methods usually aim to help comprehension for people with limited reading skills, and this audience may not overlap with AR users. Second, these methods were not designed or fine-tuned for AR-specific constraints, like the small FoV, the restricted display area, or the fact that users need to do physical tasks while they read. Third, text simplification is an opportunity to use spatial information in AR content, by describing a physical object's color, location, or direction. For example, saying the location of a physical object in the text can help users execute tasks in AR.

So we aim to implement a text simplification system for AR by tailoring existing methods to the AR context. The goal is to reduce the cognitive load of users and improve their task performance. For this we build on insights from prior work and on our own formative study, to understand the specific challenges of AR text interfaces and also their limitations and potentials. The formative study has three parts: a literature survey, an open-ended exploration, and an expert interview. We found that participants and experts both talked about issues related to reading challenges caused by long text (e.g., cognitive load) and about comprehension. From the interviews with participants and experts we got three design guidelines, and these helped us build ARTiST. ARTiST is an automated text simplification system that uses few-shot prompting. It uses the multi-task capabilities of the large language model (LLM) GPT-3 together with our newly formed simplification techniques, so extensively annotated data is not needed. We made prompts based on chain-of-thought principles, taking text simplification in AR into account. ARTiST introduces two novel simplification methods, the "plan-of-technique" prompt and "error-aware" model calibration, which make text simplification more effective and reliable.

We tested ARTiST in two studies, an empirical evaluation with 16 participants. The first study had task guidance for making pour-over coffee and for setting up a meeting room according to specific criteria. In the second study participants did video editing on an iPad, using AR instructions that were given through the HMD. The studies look at how our system can benefit participants more than the unmodified text and existing methods, by assessing performance metrics, cognitive load, and subjective ratings. The results show that ARTiST significantly improved task guidance performance. It reduced the number of errors participants made, increased the number of steps they correctly memorized, and reduced their cognitive load.

In summary, our contributions are:

- (1) ARTiST, a novel system for text simplification in AR that uses few-shot prompts and customized GPT-3. The system uses chain-of-thought, plan-of-technique, and error-aware calibration to tailor text simplification to AR.

- (2) Results and design guidelines from a formative study on text simplification in AR, which includes a literature review, an open-ended exploration with seven participants, and an expert interview with three field experts.

- (3) An empirical evaluation with 16 participants of ARTiST against baseline and existing methods. It shows that ARTiST significantly reduces errors and overall cognitive load, and users also gave it similarly higher subjective ratings on text readability, memorability, guidance, and trust.

We also open-source our implementation to support the development of the field.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Augmented reality (AR) has evolved into a transformative technology with applications across many domains, including education [1,2,3], entertainment [4,5,6,7], collaborative work [8,9,10], and professional training [11,9,12,13]. In particular, AR superimposes digital content onto the physical world in real-time, which facilitates more efficient task execution [14,15]. As a result, AR applications are increasingly employed for task guidance in manufacturing [16,17], education [18], and surgery [6]. In the manufacturing industry, for example, AR devices have been widely adopted to reduce reliance on guidance materials or other devices outside of the immediate work environment [19].

A head-mounted display (HMD) is a type of AR device that allows multi-modal interactions while the user maintains focus on the immediate work environment [19,20]. Because they are hands-free, HMDs are frequently used for text-based task guidance. However, HMDs have a relatively small field of view (FoV) compared to desktop displays, which limits the amount of text they can display; longer instructions may occlude a user’s view, resulting in lower productivity and higher cognitive load [21], as well as safety risks [6]. AR text-based instructions therefore require optimization for better utility.

Text simplification offers one potential solution. It has historically been used to reduce the complexity or length of text for users [22] in non-AR settings, making the text easier to understand. To the best of our knowledge, however, there are currently no established methods for adapting and simplifying text for the specific context of AR, and applying existing methods to AR raises several concerns. First, traditional text simplification methods typically aim to facilitate comprehension for individuals with limited reading skills [23,24], an audience that may not overlap with the AR userbase. Second, these methods have not been designed or fine-tuned for AR-specific constraints, such as the small FoV, a restricted display area, or the need for users to perform physical tasks while reading [6]. Finally, text simplification presents an opportunity to use spatial information in AR content by describing a physical object’s color, location, or direction. Indicating the location of a physical object in the text can, for example, assist users in AR task execution [6,16].

Accordingly, we aim to implement a text simplification system for AR by tailoring existing methods to the AR context, with the goal of reducing users’ cognitive load and improving their task performance. To do so, we build on insights from prior work [25,23,22,26] and our own formative study to understand the specific challenges of AR text interfaces as well as their limitations and potentials. The formative study consists of three parts: a literature survey, an open-ended exploration, and an expert interview. We found that both participants and experts raised issues related to reading challenges caused by long text (e.g., cognitive load) and to comprehension. The interviews with participants and experts also produced three design guidelines that helped build ARTiST, an automated text simplification system with few-shot prompting. The system leverages the multi-task capabilities of the large language model (LLM) GPT-3 together with our newly formed simplification techniques, which eliminates the need for extensively annotated data [27]. We crafted prompts based on chain-of-thought principles, with text simplification in AR in mind [28]. Specifically, ARTiST introduces two novel simplification methods, the “plan-of-technique” prompt and “error-aware” model calibration, which enhance the effectiveness and reliability of text simplification.

We tested ARTiST in two studies comprising an empirical evaluation with 16 participants. The first study included task guidance for making pour-over coffee and for setting up a meeting room according to specific criteria. The second study asked participants to perform video editing on an iPad using AR instructions given through an HMD. These studies explore how our system can better benefit participants compared to the unmodified text and existing methods, by assessing related performance metrics, cognitive load, and subjective ratings. The results show that ARTiST significantly improved task guidance performance by reducing the number of errors participants made, increasing the number of steps they correctly memorized, and reducing their cognitive load.

In summary, we contribute:

- (1) ARTiST, a novel system for text simplification in AR using few-shot prompts and customized GPT-3. The system incorporates chain-of-thought, plan-of-technique, and error-aware calibration to tailor text simplification to AR.

- (2) Results and design guidelines from a formative study on text simplification in AR, which includes a literature review, an open-ended exploration with seven participants, and an expert interview with three field experts.

- (3) A 16-participant empirical evaluation of ARTiST against baseline and existing methods, showing that ARTiST significantly reduces errors and overall cognitive load, with similarly higher subjective ratings from users on text readability, memorability, guidance, and trust.

To further support the development of the field, we open-source our implementation.
